newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Gilts await international money flow.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Gilts await international money flow.

text.p: International investors who have been shy of the gilt market during sterling's spectacular rise may return to gilts in the next few weeks, particularly if interest rates are left on hold, economists said on Tuesday.
"In the last couple of months a lot of investors have remained on the sidelines as they haven't fully worked out the Labour government," said Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Europe in London.

"Much of the activity we have seen since the election has been speculative. But if the Bank of England leaves rates on hold and the inflation report (on August 13) is favourable, money will come in against a fairly subdued backround of issuance," he added.

Sterling fell on Monday, partly prompted by talk the Bank of England monetary policy committee will hold off on another interest rate rise when it meets next week. The pound remained below 3.0 marks at 2.9966/76 at 0947 GMT on Tuesday.
Consumer credit data released on Tuesday showed a rise of 1.275 billion pounds in June, the highest monthly rise since the monthly series begain in 1993.
But markets and analysts are reconsidering their views that the Bank of England will implement a further succession of rate rises to curb growth.
The short sterling futures strip is discounting money market rates of around 7.25 percent all the way out to March 2000, against current official British interest rates of 6.75 percent.
"There was a feeling that interest rates were going to go up, but the appreciation of sterling has been equivalent to several points on base rates," said one senior salesman from a UK brokerage.
"We have already had tightening and we are not going to get more than another quarter point on rates -- you should be buying the short end of the gilt market," he added.

Sterling rose from a low of 2.7240 marks on May 12, following the UK election on May 1, to a high of 3.0878 marks on July 23. The newly-independent Bank of England has added 0.75 points to interest rates since the election.
This week's fall in sterling will have little direct effect on gilts, the gilt salesman said.
"The gilt future has traded around 115-11 for the past five days, with sterling both higher and lower than it is at the moment."
September gilts were trading at 115-11 at 1033 GMT, up 5/32 on the day.
The bond market will be helped in the next few weeks by the Bank of England's announcement earlier in July that it would not hold a gilt auction in August, economists said.
"With no issuance, stock is difficult to get and there could be a squeeze in August," said Briscoe.
But longer-term, prospects for gilts are less rosy, analysts said.
"The factors that have been driving sterling up are almost all still in place," said Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel in London.
"This is just a round of profit-taking. I would see sterling being pushed yet higher, with downside risks for gilts on a six to 12 month view."
